subject: physics

items.q: A single steady force is applied to a gate that can swing freely on its hinges. In which case does the gate rotate?
items.correct: When the line of action of the force does not pass through the hinges
items.misconception: Only when a second force acts on the gate at the same moment
items.why: The clearest turning actions students meet are two-handed ones - steering wheels, taps, screw tops - so they generalise that turning needs a pair of forces, and earlier work on resultant forces has trained them to link a single force with straight-line motion. The specification states that a force or a system of forces may cause an object to rotate. One force is enough, provided its line of action is some perpendicular distance from the pivot: a single push on the edge of a gate swings it about its hinges.
items.random_wrong: Whenever the force is larger than the weight of the gate itself

items.q: Which of these is an example of a force causing an object to rotate?
items.correct: Pushing on the edge of a revolving door to make it turn
items.misconception: A crate being pulled along a level floor by a rope tied to it
items.why: The clearest turning actions students meet are two-handed ones - steering wheels, taps, screw tops - so they generalise that turning needs a pair of forces, and earlier work on resultant forces has trained them to link a single force with straight-line motion. The specification states that a force or a system of forces may cause an object to rotate. One force is enough, provided its line of action is some perpendicular distance from the pivot: a single push on the edge of a gate swings it about its hinges.
items.random_wrong: Two people pushing a stalled car forwards along a flat road

items.q: A force acts on a bar that can turn about a pivot. What is the turning effect of that force called?
items.correct: The moment of the force about the pivot
items.misconception: The rotational force of the bar at the pivot
items.why: The word 'force' appears inside the phrase 'moment of a force', and students meet 'per' units such as N/kg and m/s so often that any two-quantity unit is assumed to be a division. The moment is a force multiplied by a distance, so its unit is a newton multiplied by a metre: the newton-metre, Nm. It is a turning effect, not a force, and is never measured in newtons.
items.random_wrong: The leverage of the force acting on the bar

items.q: The size of the moment of a force is defined by which equation?
items.correct: moment of a force = force × distance
items.misconception: moment of a force = weight × distance
items.why: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the kilogram figure is the number printed in the question, so it is the one students reach for. The specification gives F in newtons. A mass in kilograms must be converted to a weight in newtons using weight = mass x gravitational field strength before it is substituted into M = F d.
items.random_wrong: moment of a force = force × length of bar

items.q: Which row gives the units to use in the equation M = F d?
items.correct: M in newton-metres, F in newtons, d in metres
items.misconception: M in newton-metres, F in grams, d in metres
items.why: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the kilogram figure is the number printed in the question, so it is the one students reach for. The specification gives F in newtons. A mass in kilograms must be converted to a weight in newtons using weight = mass x gravitational field strength before it is substituted into M = F d.
items.random_wrong: M in newtons, F in newtons, d in metres

items.q: A 2.0 kg bag hangs from a beam at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from the pivot. The gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the moment of the bag's weight about the pivot?
items.correct: 5.9 Nm
items.why: Mass and weight are used interchangeably in everyday speech, and the kilogram figure is the number printed in the question, so it is the one students reach for. The specification gives F in newtons. A mass in kilograms must be converted to a weight in newtons using weight = mass x gravitational field strength before it is substituted into M = F d.

items.q: In the equation M = F d, what exactly is the distance d?
items.correct: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action
items.misconception: The distance measured along the object from the pivot to where it acts
items.why: Diagrams in textbooks usually show the force at right angles to the bar, where the two distances happen to be equal, so students never have to separate them and read d as 'distance along the bar'. The specification defines d as the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. Extend the line of action, then measure from the pivot at right angles to it; only when the force is perpendicular to the bar does this equal the distance along the bar.
items.random_wrong: The distance the object moves in the direction of the force as it turns

items.q: A 60 N push is applied to a door along a line of action that passes exactly through the hinge. Why does the door not turn?
items.correct: The perpendicular distance from the hinge is zero
items.misconception: The push is too small to overcome the weight of the door
items.why: Students treat 'force' and 'turning effect' as the same idea, so a large number for F feels as though it must produce a large turning effect regardless of where the force acts. The moment depends on the product F d. If the line of action passes through the pivot then d = 0 and the moment is zero, which is why pushing a door close to its hinge is so ineffective.
items.random_wrong: A single force can never make a heavy object rotate

items.q: A force of 25 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 15 cm from a pivot. What is the moment of the force about the pivot?
items.why: In many earlier calculations the units given already matched the equation, so students are not in the habit of checking, and 'centimetres' and 'metres' both look like ordinary length units on the page. The specification states that d is in metres and M is in newton-metres. Convert every distance to metres before substituting: 15 cm = 0.15 m gives 3.75 Nm, a hundred times smaller than the unconverted answer.

items.q: A gardener prises up a stone using a long-handled spade as a lever. Why is a long handle better than a short one?
items.correct: The same push acts at a greater distance, so its moment is larger
items.misconception: The longer handle increases the size of the push the gardener makes
items.why: The effect felt by the user is 'it feels easier', which students explain by saying the tool gives them more force, since force is the only quantity they have language for. The force you apply is unchanged; it is the distance d that increases, and M = F d then gives a larger moment. Levers transmit and increase the turning effect, not the force you exert.
items.random_wrong: The lever gives out more energy than the gardener puts into it

items.q: An object is balanced about a pivot. Which statement must be true?
items.correct: The total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment
items.misconception: The total of the forces on one side equals the total on the other side
items.why: Adding forces is what students practise for months in work on resultant forces, so a balance problem triggers the familiar routine before the new one. Balance is a condition on moments, not on forces. Each force must first be multiplied by its own distance from the pivot; only then are the clockwise and anticlockwise totals compared.
items.random_wrong: Each force must act the same distance from the pivot as the other one

items.q: A plank balances on a pivot. A 10 N weight sits 0.60 m to the left of the pivot, and a 30 N weight sits somewhere to the right. What can be said about the 30 N weight?
items.correct: It sits closer to the pivot, because its force is the larger
items.misconception: It sits further from the pivot, because a larger force turns more
items.why: Students reason from the force alone rather than from the product F d, so 'bigger force' is taken to imply 'bigger everything', including distance. Since the moments are equal and moment = force x distance, the larger force must act at the smaller distance. That is exactly how a crowbar works: a small effort far out balances a large load close in.
items.random_wrong: It sits the same distance out, as the plank is balanced

items.q: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 100 N weight hangs 0.75 m to the left of the pivot, and a single weight hangs 1.5 m to the right. What is that weight?
items.why: Adding forces is what students practise for months in work on resultant forces, so a balance problem triggers the familiar routine before the new one. Balance is a condition on moments, not on forces. Each force must first be multiplied by its own distance from the pivot; only then are the clockwise and anticlockwise totals compared.

items.q: A rod is balanced on a pivot. A 6.0 N force acts 0.50 m from the pivot on one side, and an 8.0 N force acts on the other side. How far from the pivot is the 8.0 N force?
items.why: Rearranging M = F d is done by pattern-matching rather than by algebra, so students pick whichever of the three operations produces a comfortable-looking number. Rearranging M = F d properly gives d = M / F and F = M / d. Checking the units helps: newton-metres divided by newtons leaves metres, which is what a distance should be.

items.q: What do a simple lever and a simple gear system have in common?
items.correct: Both can be used to transmit the rotational effects of forces
items.misconception: Both give out more energy than is put into them by the user
items.why: The visible outcome, a small person shifting a heavy load, looks like a gain, and students have no accounting rule that stops them treating machines as sources of extra effect. The lever transmits the rotational effect of the force; it does not create it. The moment of the effort about the pivot is what moves the load, and the effort must move through a much greater distance than the load does.
items.random_wrong: Both increase the size of the force that you apply to them

items.q: Two gear wheels are meshed together and the smaller one is driven clockwise. How does the larger gear turn?
items.correct: Anticlockwise, more slowly, and with a larger moment
items.misconception: Clockwise too, because the teeth push it the same way round
items.why: Students picture the rotation being handed on unchanged, as it is by a belt or a chain, and do not look at the direction in which the teeth actually push at the point of contact. At the point where the teeth mesh, the surfaces of the two wheels move together, which sends the second wheel round the opposite way. A chain or belt drive keeps the sense the same; meshed teeth reverse it.
items.random_wrong: Anticlockwise but faster, because it is the bigger wheel

items.q: Two children balance on a see-saw. What must be true about their weights and their distances from the pivot?
items.correct: Their moments must be equal: weight x distance on one side equals weight x distance on the other. The weights themselves need not be equal, nor the distances.
items.misconception: If it is balanced then the two children must weigh the same, or must be sitting the same distance out from the pivot.
items.why: Playground see-saws are usually used by children of similar size sitting at the ends, so the balanced cases students actually see are the symmetrical ones, and 'balanced' gets read as 'the same on both sides'. The condition is on the moments, not on the forces or the distances separately. A light child far from the pivot balances a heavy child close to it, because the two products weight x distance are equal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A small gear wheel drives a larger gear wheel meshed with it. How does the larger gear turn?
items.correct: More slowly than the small gear, and with a larger moment, because it has more teeth to move round for each turn of the small one.
items.misconception: The bigger gear turns faster because it is bigger, or both gears turn at the same rate because they are joined together.
items.why: Students see the rim of the large wheel sweeping a long way and read that as 'faster', and 'joined together' suggests the two wheels must do the same thing. The teeth mesh, so both gears pass the same number of teeth per second. The larger wheel therefore completes fewer turns per second, and it turns with a larger moment than the smaller driving gear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A moment of 5.0 is calculated from a 25 N force at 0.20 m. Can the answer be given in joules?
items.correct: No. The moment of a force is given in newton-metres, Nm. Joules are the unit of energy and work done.
items.misconception: Work done is force x distance and a moment is force x distance, so they are the same thing and either unit will do.
items.why: The two equations look identical on the page, and students match equations by their shape rather than by what the distances in them mean. In work done, the distance is measured along the direction of the force; in a moment, it is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. They are different quantities, so the moment is given in Nm, not J.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A metre rule is balanced with the pivot at the 30 cm mark. Is this possible?
items.correct: Yes. Moments can be taken about any pivot, and a balanced object need not be symmetrical about it.
items.misconception: A balanced object has to be symmetrical - the pivot in the middle and each force the same distance out.
items.why: Almost every first example of balance is a symmetrical see-saw, so symmetry becomes part of what students think 'balanced' means. The condition is that the total clockwise moment about the pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment about that pivot. Any arrangement satisfying that is balanced, symmetrical or not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
